title: Stoichiometry and Limiting Reagent
subcategory: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry — Stoichiometry, Limiting Reagent

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 11 — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

summary: Stoichiometry uses a balanced equation's mole ratios to relate amounts of reactants and products; when reactants aren't in the exact stoichiometric ratio, the limiting reagent (fully consumed first) determines the maximum possible product.
explanation: A balanced chemical equation's coefficients give the mole ratio in which reactants combine and products form — this ratio, not the mass ratio, is what stoichiometric calculations are built on, since moles directly count particles/formula units while mass depends on molar mass too. In practice, reactants are rarely mixed in exactly the stoichiometric ratio; the LIMITING REAGENT is whichever reactant gets completely used up first, and it alone determines the maximum amount of product that CAN form — any reactant left over is called the excess reagent. To identify the limiting reagent, divide the available moles of each reactant by its stoichiometric coefficient; the reactant giving the SMALLEST value is limiting. Theoretical yield is the maximum product mass/moles calculated purely from stoichiometry (assuming the reaction goes to completion with no losses); actual yield is what is really obtained in an experiment (always ≤ theoretical, due to side reactions, incomplete reactions, or losses during handling). Percentage yield = (actual yield/theoretical yield) × 100, a practical measure of a reaction's real-world efficiency. Related mole-based ideas — empirical formula (simplest whole-number ratio of atoms) versus molecular formula (actual number of atoms, an integer multiple of the empirical formula) — also depend entirely on correctly converting given masses/percentages to moles first.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the reactant present in the smaller MASS is automatically the limiting reagent — limiting reagent is decided by moles relative to the STOICHIOMETRIC RATIO, not by raw mass or even raw moles alone.
Calculating product amounts using the excess reagent's quantity instead of the limiting reagent's — this always overestimates the actual product formed.

Believing percentage yield can exceed 100% under ideal conditions — a value over 100% signals an experimental/measurement error (e.g. impure product, calculation mistake), never a genuinely 'better than theoretical' result.
examples: If 2 mol H₂ reacts with 1 mol O₂ to form water (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O), the reactants are in the exact stoichiometric ratio and both are fully consumed together.
Mixing 4 mol H₂ with 1 mol O₂ for the same reaction leaves O₂ as limiting (needs only 2 mol H₂), with 2 mol H₂ left unreacted (excess).
genZNote: Limiting reagent: the one reactant that ghosts the reaction early and ruins everyone else's plans.
